metadata.title: QRNG Art — art from quantum noise
metadata.description: A unique image every day, generated from quantum random numbers. Australian National University, ANU QRNG.
metadata.ogAlt: QRNG Art — art from quantum noise

home.title: Art of the Day
home.paragraph1: This image was not drawn by an artist or made by an AI model. It grew out of 1000 numbers of true quantum randomness from the Australian National University’s generator (ANU QRNG), which measures quantum fluctuations of the vacuum. No algorithm computes these numbers, so they are genuinely unpredictable.
home.paragraph2: The numbers decide everything: which of 15 scenes appears today — from desert and fjord to Belgrade and a Japanese garden — the palette and time of day, what is in the frame, and whether something rare shows up, like a rainbow, a comet or an eclipse. Small details (stars, raindrops, blades of grass) are drawn by a generator seeded with the same numbers.
home.paragraph3: The same numbers always produce the same image. Today’s numbers are shown above, and every earlier image waits in the archive.
home.paragraph4Suffix: shows all 15 scenes and 9 abstractions from the same numbers and lets you tweak them.

algorithmic.title: Algorithmic Art
algorithmic.subtitle: QRNG values as the engine of generative algorithms
algorithmic.errorRandom: Unable to load QRNG values. Please try again.
algorithmic.errorToday: Unable to load today's art. Please try again.
algorithmic.storyIntro: Every abstraction reads the same 1000 quantum numbers in order. The numbers set the starting conditions: positions, angles and colours. The palette and sliders only shape the algorithm and don't consume numbers, so the same numbers with the same settings always give the same image.
algorithmic.storyFlowField: Controls: 5 (palette + particles, speed, trail width, trail opacity). From the batch: 336 field angles (24×14 grid) + 4 values per particle for start position, age, and lifespan — total 336 + 4×particle count (e.g. 600 particles ≈ 2736 draws).
algorithmic.storyWave: Controls: 4 (palette + wave count, amplitude, contrast). From the batch: 4 values per wave (frequencies, phase, wave amplitude) + 1 for glow count + 3 per glow — roughly 4×n + 10 to 19 draws, where n is the wave count (4–24).
algorithmic.storyVoronoi: Controls: 3 (palette + cell count, border width). From the batch: 5 values per Voronoi site — RGB jitter and x,y — total 5×n, with n from 20 to 400.
algorithmic.storyLSystem: Controls: 4 (palette + depth, angle, length factor). From the batch: 1 for a slight horizontal offset + 2 per F segment (angle and length jitter) + 1 per + or − symbol. Draw count grows quickly with depth (e.g. depth 5 ≈ 730, depth 7 ≈ 6500).
algorithmic.storyCellular: Controls: 3 (palette + rule, cell size). From the batch: one value per column of the initial row — column count is canvas width divided by cell size (up to about 1200 at the smallest cell size).
algorithmic.storyTruchet: Controls: 3 (palette + tile size, line width). From the batch: one draw per tile for rotation (0° or 90°). If the total tile count is below ~800, an extra draw per tile decides a rare glow overlay.
algorithmic.storyJulia: Controls: 3 (palette + max iterations, zoom). From the batch: exactly the first 4 values — two for the real and imaginary parts of c, two for a small perturbation.
algorithmic.storyNewton: Controls: 4 (palette + polynomial degree, max iterations, zoom). From the batch: exactly 2×degree successive values for initial root positions in the complex plane (degree 3–7 → 6 to 14 draws).
algorithmic.storyApollonian: Controls: 4 (palette + maximum circle count, minimum radius, line width). Starts from four circles with curvatures −1, 2, 2, 3; the first 12 values of the stream gently perturb curvatures and centres. New circles come from Descartes' theorem (centres as complex numbers), and triples expand breadth-first until the maximum circle count or minimum radius is reached. Colour depends on depth and a pattern from the stream.
algorithmic.errorLoadFavorite: Unable to load this favorite. It may have been removed or you may not have access.
algorithmic.storyStream: When an algorithm needs more than 1000 values, each extra value comes from XOR-ing a deterministic PRNG output with the original quantum numbers, cycling from the start. Quantum entropy stays present throughout the whole stream.
algorithmic.aboutFlowField: An invisible grid of arrows tells each particle where to go, and thousands of particles leave trails like wind or ocean currents. The same technique draws wind maps in weather forecasts. The quantum numbers set the direction of every arrow and where the particles start, so no two fields are alike.
algorithmic.aboutWave: Several waves of different frequencies add up into one surface, like ripples crossing on water. Where they line up you get bright crests, and where they cancel, dark troughs. This is called interference. The quantum numbers choose each wave's frequency, phase and strength.
algorithmic.aboutVoronoi: The plane is split into cells so that every point belongs to its nearest seed. Nature makes the same shapes: leaf cells, giraffe patterns, cracks in dried mud. The quantum numbers place every seed and give it a slightly different colour.
algorithmic.aboutLSystem: An L-system is a small set of rules that biologist Aristid Lindenmayer devised in 1968 to describe how plants grow: a branch splits into smaller branches, a few times over, until a whole tree appears. The quantum numbers slightly change the angle and length of each branch, so the tree looks alive rather than perfectly symmetric.
algorithmic.aboutCellular: A row of cells that are on or off, and each next row follows from the previous one by a simple rule. Stephen Wolfram catalogued all 256 such rules: some draw Sierpiński triangles, others pure chaos. The quantum numbers set only the first row, and everything below follows from the rule.
algorithmic.aboutTruchet: Square tiles with two arcs that can sit in two orientations, studied by Sébastien Truchet as early as 1704. One tile is dull, but together the arcs join into endless winding paths. The quantum numbers turn every tile.
algorithmic.aboutJulia: For every point of the plane the formula z → z² + c is repeated, watching whether the value escapes to infinity. The border between escaping and staying points is a fractal, with new detail at every zoom. Gaston Julia described it in 1918. The quantum numbers choose the constant c, and even a tiny change in c transforms the shape.
algorithmic.aboutNewton: Newton's method searches for the roots of a polynomial step by step. Every point of the plane takes the colour of the root it reaches, and along the borders, where the method can't decide, endlessly branching patterns appear. The quantum numbers place the roots of the polynomial.
algorithmic.aboutApollonian: Between three touching circles there is always room for exactly one new circle that touches all three. Apollonius of Perga knew this around 200 BC, and Descartes' theorem gives the size of the new circle. Repeating it fills the circle with ever smaller circles. The quantum numbers slightly shift the starting circles and choose the colours.

sceneStory.title: About this scene
sceneStory.intro: The first four quantum numbers pick the scene, and all the following ones choose the palette, the light and the scene's elements: where the tree stands, whether there is lightning, how many birds fly by.
sceneStory.technicalText: Scene choice: (v0 ⊕ v1 ⊕ v2 ⊕ v3) mod 15, so each scene has about a 6.7% chance. In the Studio you can also pick the scene by hand: the numbers still choose everything else, and the scene controls change only the element you pick while the rest of the image stays the same.
sceneStory.s0: A low-poly mountain range: sharp snow-capped peaks rise from a sea of clouds above foothills and an alpine meadow. The shape of every peak and the colour of every triangle come from the quantum numbers.
sceneStory.s1: A tropical beach with turquoise shallows, foam on the shore, palm trees and cumulus clouds over the open sea. Sometimes an island or a sailboat appears on the horizon.
sceneStory.s2: The sun over the open sea at different heights, from golden hour to blue hour. Clouds catch the last light and a path of light stretches across the water. The sky has eight palettes.
sceneStory.s3: Dunes with a sharp edge between light and shadow and mesas on the horizon, sometimes with a caravan, an oasis or a saguaro cactus. At night the Milky Way rises over the sand.
sceneStory.s4: A city at night in three layers of buildings, with windows lit floor by floor. Above, a full moon or a crescent; in front, a river with reflections or a street.
sceneStory.s5: A view into space: a nebula, stars with spikes, a galaxy and planets of five types, some with rings and moons, sometimes in close-up.
sceneStory.s6: A clearing or a forested valley in mist, with firs, broadleaf trees and sunbeams through the canopy. Sometimes a deer or fireflies appear.
sceneStory.s7: A mountain lake with a true reflection of peaks and forest and mist over the water. Sometimes snow, a pier, a boat or reeds.
sceneStory.s8: A view across the river to one of three cities mirrored in the water: Belgrade (Saint Sava Temple, Ušće, Avala, Kalemegdan), Paris (Eiffel Tower, Sacré-Cœur, Notre-Dame) or Rome (St. Peter's, the Colosseum, Castel Sant'Angelo).
sceneStory.s9: A coral reef with kelp, schools of fish, tropical fish, a turtle and jellyfish, lit by rays from the surface. Or the abyss, where only bioluminescent creatures and an anglerfish glow.
sceneStory.s10: A huge low sun, acacias and a baobab, giraffes, elephants, antelopes or zebras, with Kilimanjaro in the distance. At sunset and at night the animals turn into silhouettes.
sceneStory.s11: Open country in one of three regions: Vojvodina (wheat, bales and a farmstead with a well sweep), Provence (a stone house) or Tuscany (rolling hills and a cypress-lined road). Crop rows run into the distance.
sceneStory.s12: A lighthouse at sea, a lone tree or mountains under layered storm clouds. Lightning branches, rain falls in curtains, and a rainbow appears as the storm passes.
sceneStory.s13: A fjord with cliffs and reflections, a cut through the water showing an iceberg and its hidden part, or an icy shore with a polar bear or penguins. A soft aurora often glows above.
sceneStory.s14: In the style of Japanese woodblock prints (ukiyo-e): four seasons, a volcano, bands of mist, a pagoda, a torii gate, an arched bridge and a pond with koi.
